headline: High risk: Goose’s default filesystem/MCP/tooling can conflict with Dagster’s orchestration context, while Dagster itself is read-only and non-runnable.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Dagster has no filesystem, clipboard, MCP, or stdin/stdout bridge, so it cannot directly inject Goose by default. Goose can ingest files and MCP outputs, but the pair lacks a documented automatic channel from Dagster to Goose. The only plausible bridge is unusual manual transfer or external wiring, so blast radius is small.
conditions: IF an operator manually copies Dagster-generated text into Goose prompts, injection becomes possible.
IF an external workflow writes Dagster output into a Goose-readable file or MCP source, Goose may parse attacker-controlled content.
mitigations: Keep Dagster outputs out of Goose prompts unless reviewed.
Disable any file-watching or auto-ingest workflow between the two.
Use a separate staging directory for Dagster artifacts.
Require human review before Goose consumes Dagster-generated text.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Dagster touches no data classes and has no filesystem or network egress, but Goose reads and writes the user filesystem and can call configured model providers and MCP servers. If Dagster artifacts contain secrets or regulated data, Goose can expose them through its default tool and provider pathways. The interaction is indirect but plausible in default use.
conditions: IF Dagster writes sensitive artifacts into the shared user filesystem, Goose can read them.
IF Goose is configured with a third-party model provider or MCP server, those contents may leave the machine.
mitigations: Store Dagster artifacts in a restricted directory.
Remove secrets from any files Goose can access.
Audit Goose provider and MCP settings before use.
Use redacted copies for any Dagster-to-Goose handoff.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Dagster is non-runnable and has no write or git capabilities, while Goose can write the filesystem, modify git state, and spawn subprocesses. There is no direct write-write conflict between the agents themselves, but Goose can mutate shared files that Dagster may later consume. Uncertainty about orchestration locking pushes this above low.
conditions: IF Goose and Dagster operate on the same workspace, Goose can overwrite files Dagster later reads.
IF Dagster is embedded in a workflow that assumes immutable inputs, Goose edits can create conflicts.
mitigations: Separate Dagster and Goose workspaces.
Use read-only mounts for Dagster inputs.
Add file-locking around shared artifacts.
Require explicit checkout/commit steps before Goose edits git state.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Dagster is an orchestrator and Goose is an action-capable coding agent with shell, git, and network access. If Dagster-produced artifacts are fed into Goose without verification, Goose may act on incorrect pipeline metadata or code. Dagster’s lack of direct execution does not eliminate the cascade because Goose can turn upstream mistakes into downstream actions.
conditions: IF Dagster output is used as authoritative input to Goose, Goose may execute incorrect actions.
IF Goose is allowed to commit or deploy based on Dagster artifacts, upstream errors can cascade.
mitigations: Insert a verification step between Dagster and Goose.
Require schema validation on Dagster outputs.
Block Goose from acting on unreviewed pipeline metadata.
Use dry-run mode for any Goose action derived from Dagster.

E_compliance.rationale: Dagster’s profile shows no touched data classes and no secrets, while Goose explicitly handles model-provider keys and extension tokens and runs as the user with broad filesystem access. This is a compliance overlap with documented gaps, but no specific residency or regulated-data mismatch is evidenced here, so the risk stays low.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed in files Goose can access, compliance obligations may be triggered.
IF Goose provider keys or extension tokens are stored alongside Dagster artifacts, retention controls may diverge.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of Goose-accessible paths.
Separate secret storage from pipeline artifacts.
Review retention settings for Goose logs and provider data.
Document which data classes may flow through each agent.
